The Cox model and its parametric cousins assume a particular shape for how covariates act on the
hazard (usually linear and proportional). When you have many covariates, non-linear effects, or
interactions you did not anticipate, tree-based machine-learning models can predict better without
those assumptions. Greenwood ships three, all fully non-parametric and all producing per-subject
survival and cumulative-hazard *functions* rather than a single risk score: a `SurvivalTree`, the
bagged `RandomSurvivalForest` (and its extremely-randomized `ExtraSurvivalTrees` variant), and
`GradientBoostingSurvivalAnalysis`. This page introduces each, then shows how to score, interpret,
and visualize them.

We'll work with `lung`-dataset outcomes, keeping the rows with complete covariates so the examples
are easy to follow.

```{python}
import greenwood as gw

# Load the lung dataset and keep rows with complete covariates
lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars").drop_nulls(
    subset=["ph.ecog", "ph.karno", "wt.loss"]
)

y = gw.Surv.right(lung["time"], event=(lung["status"] == 2))
covariates = ["age", "sex", "ph.ecog", "ph.karno", "wt.loss"]
y
```

## Survival trees

A `SurvivalTree` recursively splits subjects into groups whose survival curves differ as much as
possible, measured by the log-rank statistic at each candidate split. Each leaf stores a
Kaplan-Meier survival curve and a Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazard estimated from the subjects that
land in it. A single tree is easy to reason about but high-variance; it is most useful as the
interpretable building block of an ensemble.

```{python}
# Grow a shallow, interpretable survival tree
tree = gw.SurvivalTree(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(y, lung[covariates])
tree
```

Calling `predict` with the default `type="risk"` returns Ishwaran's *ensemble mortality* (the sum
of the predicted cumulative hazard over the training event times). Larger values mean higher risk.

```{python}
# Risk score for the first eight subjects (higher = higher risk)
tree.predict(lung[covariates])[:8]
```

## Random survival forests

A `RandomSurvivalForest` averages many decorrelated survival trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample
of the data and considering a random subset of covariates at every split. Averaging drives down the
variance of the single tree and yields a well-calibrated, flexible model. Passing `oob_score=True`
computes an out-of-bag concordance estimate (an honest, held-out measure of discrimination) using
only the trees for which each subject was not in the bootstrap sample.

```{python}
# Fit a forest and report the out-of-bag concordance
rsf = gw.RandomSurvivalForest(
    n_estimators=200, oob_score=True, random_state=0
).fit(y, lung[covariates])
rsf
```

### Predictions

Like the tree, the forest predicts a scalar risk score by default. It also predicts full survival or
cumulative-hazard curves: pass `type="survival"` (or `"cumulative_hazard"`) and optional `times`, and
you get one column per subject.

```{python}
# Predicted survival probabilities at one and two years for three subjects
rsf.predict(lung[covariates][:3], type="survival", times=[365, 730])
```

### Variable importance

`variable_importance()` measures how much each covariate contributes by permuting its values in the
out-of-bag samples and recording the drop in concordance. Larger values indicate more important
covariates. The same table is what `tidy()` returns for a fitted forest.

```{python}
# Permutation variable importance (out-of-bag)
rsf.variable_importance()
```

## Extra survival trees

`ExtraSurvivalTrees` is an extremely-randomized variant: in addition to sampling covariates, it
draws the split *threshold* at random for each candidate rather than optimizing it. The extra
randomness further decorrelates the trees, often lowering variance and speeding up fitting.
Following the extra-trees convention, it grows each tree on the whole sample by default; set
`bootstrap=True` when you want out-of-bag scoring or variable importance.

```{python}
# Extremely-randomized survival trees with out-of-bag scoring enabled
ext = gw.ExtraSurvivalTrees(
    n_estimators=200, bootstrap=True, oob_score=True, random_state=0
).fit(y, lung[covariates])
ext
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Accelerating the split search on large data

The best-split search is the dominant cost when fitting forests on large datasets. If you install
the `fast` extra (`pip install greenwood[fast]`), you can pass `engine="numba"` to
`RandomSurvivalForest` or `ExtraSurvivalTrees` for a compiled split kernel that avoids materializing
the large risk-set matrices. The default `engine="numpy"` is deterministic and needs no extra
dependency; the Numba path produces a statistically equivalent fit that may differ slightly in
tie-breaking.
:::

## Gradient-boosted survival

`GradientBoostingSurvivalAnalysis` takes a different route. Instead of averaging independent trees,
it builds an additive model by fitting each new (shallow) regression tree to the negative gradient
of the Cox partial-likelihood loss (the martingale residuals under the current model) and adding a
shrunken version of it. The result is a non-linear generalization of the Cox model that often
predicts very well on structured tabular data.

```{python}
# Fit a gradient-boosted survival model
gbm = gw.GradientBoostingSurvivalAnalysis(
    n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=2, random_state=0
).fit(y, lung[covariates])
gbm
```

The additive score `F(x)` is the boosted analogue of the Cox linear predictor. `predict(type="lp")`
returns it, `type="risk"` returns `exp(F(x))`, and `type="survival"` combines it with a Breslow
baseline hazard to produce survival curves.

```{python}
# Survival curves at one and two years for three subjects
gbm.predict(lung[covariates][:3], type="survival", times=[365, 730])
```

Boosting reports impurity-based variable importance (the total reduction in squared error credited
to each covariate, normalized to sum to one):

```{python}
# Impurity-based variable importance
gbm.variable_importance()
```

## IPC-weighted ridge regression

Not every alternative to Cox needs a tree. `IPCRidge` fits a penalized linear model on log survival
times, but instead of the Cox partial likelihood it uses inverse-probability-of-censoring (IPC)
weights to correct for censoring. Only uncensored subjects contribute to the fit, and each is
weighted by 1 / G(t-) from the Kaplan-Meier censoring estimate so that subjects whose events occur
when censoring is heavy receive greater influence. The result is a simple linear model that does not
assume proportional hazards.

```{python}
ridge = gw.IPCRidge(alpha=1.0).fit(y, lung[covariates])
ridge
```

The `alpha` parameter controls the ridge penalty. Setting `alpha=0` gives unpenalized IPC-weighted
OLS. Larger values shrink the coefficients toward zero, which helps when covariates are correlated
or numerous.

Predictions are on the log-time scale by default (`type="lp"`). Pass `type="response"` to get
predicted survival times on the original scale.

```{python}
ridge.predict(lung[covariates][:5], type="response")
```

The coefficient table is available via `tidy()`, and model-level summaries via `glance()`.

```{python}
gw.tidy(ridge)
```

```{python}
gw.glance(ridge)
```

Because the linear predictor is on the log-time scale (higher means longer survival), negate it to
get a risk score compatible with `concordance_index()`.

```{python}
risk = -ridge.predict(lung[covariates], type="lp")
gw.concordance_index(y, risk)
```

## Visualizing per-subject curves

Because these models predict an individual survival curve for every subject,
`plot_predicted_survival()` draws one step curve per row of new data. It works with any of the
machine-learning models (and with `CoxPH`), so you can compare how predicted survival varies across
individuals.

```{python}
# Compare predicted survival for four patients from the forest
gw.plot_predicted_survival(rsf, lung[covariates][:4])
```

Pass `type="cumulative_hazard"` for the cumulative-hazard scale, or `labels=` to name the curves.

## Comparing models

All of these models expose a risk score, so you can judge and compare them with the same
censoring-aware metrics as any other model. Here we compare the three ensembles by concordance on
the training data (for an honest estimate, evaluate on held-out data or use the forest's out-of-bag
score).

```{python}
# In-sample concordance for the three ensemble models
scores = {
    "random forest": gw.concordance_index(y, rsf.predict(lung[covariates])),
    "extra trees": gw.concordance_index(y, ext.predict(lung[covariates])),
    "gradient boosting": gw.concordance_index(y, gbm.predict(lung[covariates])),
}
scores
```

See [Prediction performance](15-prediction-performance.qmd) for concordance on held-out data, the
Brier score, and time-dependent AUC (the right way to compare these models).

## SurvivalBoost: competing-risks gradient boosting

The models above apply to single-event survival data. When you have **competing risks**, where
subjects can experience one of several mutually exclusive event types, `SurvivalBoost` is the
machine-learning counterpart. It estimates cause-specific cumulative incidence functions (CIFs) and
the any-event survival function directly, using multi-class softmax gradient boosting with
IPCW-weighted targets. The approach follows Alberge et al. (2025).

### How it works

At each boosting iteration, `SurvivalBoost` samples random time horizons and appends them as an
extra feature column alongside the original covariates. For every subject-horizon pair, it computes
a multi-class target: event type $k$ if cause $k$ occurred before the horizon, or "event-free" if
the subject was still at risk. Subjects censored before the horizon receive zero weight and are
excluded. Uncensored subjects are reweighted by the inverse probability of censoring (IPCW) to
correct for informative dropout.

The model then fits one regression tree per class to the softmax gradient residuals of the current
ensemble, exactly as in multi-class gradient boosting for tabular data. Because the time horizon
varies from iteration to iteration, the ensemble learns how the class probabilities evolve over time
without being tied to a fixed grid. Predictions are probability-calibrated by construction: the
softmax output sums to one at every time point.

The `hard_zero_fraction` parameter forces a fraction of time horizons to exactly zero each iteration.
This teaches the model that no events have occurred at $t = 0$, preventing CIFs from starting at a
nonzero value.

### Fitting the model

`SurvivalBoost` consumes a multi-state `Surv` response (from `Surv.multistate()`) and a covariate
matrix. We use `simulate_competing_risks()` to generate synthetic data with known properties, but
the model works with any competing-risks dataset.

```{python}
import numpy as np

# Generate competing-risks data: 2 causes, 3 covariates
sim = gw.simulate_competing_risks(n=500, n_causes=2, n_covariates=3, seed=42)

# Fit SurvivalBoost
sb = gw.SurvivalBoost(
    n_estimators=50, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3, random_state=0
)
sb.fit(sim.surv, sim.covariates)
sb
```

The fitted model reports the number of subjects, events, causes, and features. Internally it stores
one set of trees per class per boosting round.

### Predicting CIFs and survival

`predict_cumulative_incidence` returns a 3-D array of shape `(n_subjects, n_classes, n_times)`.
Index 0 along the class axis is the survival probability (the probability that no event has occurred
by time $t$). Indices 1 through $K$ are the cause-specific CIFs.

```{python}
times = np.array([2.0, 5.0, 10.0, 15.0])
cif = sb.predict_cumulative_incidence(sim.covariates, times=times)
cif.shape
```

Because the predictions pass through a softmax, the probabilities always sum to one across classes
at every time point. That means the survival probability is exactly `1 - sum(CIFs)`, which is the
correct accounting for competing risks.

```{python}
# Verify: probabilities sum to 1 at each time for every subject
cif.sum(axis=1)[:3, :]
```

The survival function alone is available via `predict_survival_function`, which returns a 2-D array
of shape `(n_subjects, n_times)`.

```{python}
surv_pred = sb.predict_survival_function(sim.covariates, times=times)
surv_pred[:3, :]  # first three subjects
```

For a classifier-style interface at a single time horizon, `predict_proba` returns a 2-D array where
each row sums to one.

```{python}
# Class probabilities at t = 8 for the first five subjects
sb.predict_proba(sim.covariates[:5], time_horizon=8.0)
```

### DataFrame output

Both prediction methods accept a `format=` parameter for DataFrame output. For
`predict_cumulative_incidence`, the result is a long-format table with columns `time`, `cause`,
`subject`, and `probability`.

```{python}
sb.predict_cumulative_incidence(
    sim.covariates[:3], times=np.array([5.0, 10.0]), format="polars"
).head(6)
```

For `predict_survival_function`, the result is a wide-format table with one column per subject,
matching the format used by `GradientBoostingSurvivalAnalysis`.

```{python}
sb.predict_survival_function(
    sim.covariates[:3], times=np.array([5.0, 10.0]), format="polars"
)
```

### Evaluating predictions

Because `SurvivalBoost` produces CIF estimates, you can evaluate them with the competing-risks
metrics from [Prediction performance](15-prediction-performance.qmd). The cause-specific Brier score
measures calibration at each time horizon. Lower values mean the predicted probabilities are closer
to the observed outcomes.

```{python}
# Brier score for cause 1 at several time horizons
eval_times = np.array([3.0, 6.0, 10.0])
cif_eval = sb.predict_cumulative_incidence(sim.covariates, times=eval_times)
bs = gw.brier_score_incidence(sim.surv, cif_eval[:, 1, :], eval_times, cause=1)
dict(zip(eval_times, bs))
```

The concordance index for incidence measures discrimination: how well the model ranks subjects by
their predicted CIF at a given time horizon. Values above 0.5 indicate better-than-random ranking.

```{python}
# Concordance for cause 1 at median follow-up
tau = float(np.median(sim.surv.stop))
cif_tau = sb.predict_cumulative_incidence(sim.covariates, times=np.array([tau]))
c_index = gw.concordance_index_incidence(sim.surv, cif_tau[:, 1, 0], cause=1, tau=tau)
c_index
```

You can also check calibration (how close the predicted CIFs are to the Aalen-Johansen reference)
and accuracy in time (classification accuracy at each horizon). See
[Prediction performance](15-prediction-performance.qmd) for details on all four metrics.

### Model summaries

`SurvivalBoost` supports the broom-style `tidy()` and `glance()` interface. `glance()` returns a
one-row summary with the model's key parameters and counts.

```{python}
gw.glance(sb)
```

### Tuning

The main hyperparameters to tune are:

- `n_estimators`: More boosting iterations improve fit up to a point, after which the model
overfits. Typical values range from 50 to 500.
- `learning_rate`: Smaller rates (0.01 to 0.1) need more iterations but generalize better. Together,
`n_estimators` and `learning_rate` control the bias-variance tradeoff.
- `max_depth`: Controls the interaction depth of each tree. Depth 2 to 4 is typical. Deeper trees
capture higher-order interactions but are more prone to overfitting.
- `subsample`: Setting this below 1.0 gives stochastic gradient boosting, where each iteration uses
a random fraction of the training data. Values around 0.8 often improve generalization.
- `n_horizons_per_observation`: The number of time horizons sampled per subject per iteration.
Higher values (3 to 5) give more stable gradients at the cost of proportionally slower training.
- `hard_zero_fraction`: Ensures the model learns zero incidence at $t = 0$. The default of 0.1 works
well in most settings. Increase it if predicted CIFs at $t = 0$ are not close to zero.

Use held-out data or `cross_validate` to select these. Because the model is non-parametric, it can
capture complex covariate effects that Fine-Gray would miss, but it also needs enough data and
regularization (depth limits, learning-rate shrinkage) to avoid overfitting.

::: {.callout-note}
## SurvivalBoost vs. Fine-Gray

Fine-Gray fits a single cause at a time and assumes a log-linear effect on the subdistribution
hazard. `SurvivalBoost` estimates all causes jointly, captures non-linear effects and interactions
automatically, and produces probability-calibrated predictions without post-processing. The tradeoff
is interpretability: Fine-Gray gives a coefficient per covariate with a clear hazard-ratio
interpretation, while `SurvivalBoost` is a black-box ensemble. When prediction accuracy matters more
than interpretability, `SurvivalBoost` is the stronger choice.
:::

### More than two causes

`SurvivalBoost` handles any number of competing event types. The number of output classes is always
$K + 1$ (one per cause, plus the survival class).

```{python}
# Three competing causes
sim3 = gw.simulate_competing_risks(n=400, n_causes=3, n_covariates=2, seed=7)
sb3 = gw.SurvivalBoost(n_estimators=30, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=2, random_state=0)
sb3.fit(sim3.surv, sim3.covariates)

# CIF at t = 5: shape is (400, 4, 1) because there are 4 classes (survival + 3 causes)
cif3 = sb3.predict_cumulative_incidence(sim3.covariates, times=np.array([5.0]))
cif3.shape
```

The model scales naturally: each additional cause adds one class to the softmax and one tree per
boosting round. The probabilities still sum to one across all classes at every time point, so the
survival function and CIFs remain mutually consistent regardless of how many causes are present.

For background on how competing risks are represented and why the cumulative incidence function is
the right estimand, see [Competing risks](13-competing-risks.qmd). For evaluating CIF predictions
with discrimination, calibration, and classification metrics, see
[Prediction performance](15-prediction-performance.qmd).
